content: A blood-borne disease refers to any disease that can be transmitted through exposure to contaminated blood. Common examples of such diseases include HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and viral hemorrhagic fevers. Diseases that are not typically spread directly through blood contact, but rather through insect or other vectors, are more accurately classified as vector-borne diseases, even though the causative agent may be present in the blood. Examples of vector-borne diseases include West Nile virus and malaria. Many blood-borne diseases can also be transmitted through other routes. Because it is challenging to determine the specific pathogens present in any given sample of blood, and because some blood-borne diseases can be fatal, standard medical practice treats all blood and bodily fluids as potentially infectious. Blood and body fluid precautions are a set of infection control measures designed to minimize the risk of transmitting these diseases. Blood intended for transfusion is routinely screened for numerous blood-borne pathogens. Needle exchange programs are implemented as a harm reduction strategy to decrease the spread of blood-borne diseases among intravenous drug users.
